en-a1-u01-l01.title: Hello!
en-a1-u01-l01.objective: By the end you can say hello, say your name and ask someone else's name.
en-a1-u01-l01.warmup: How do you greet someone new in your language? Now let's see how it's done in English.
en-a1-u01-l01.topic: To be: I am / you are
md: **I'm = I am**. In English the subject is always needed: *I'm Anna*, not *Am Anna*.
**What's your name?** = *What is your name?* You can answer *I'm Anna* or *My name is Anna*.
| Informal | More formal |
| Hi! | Hello! |
| Bye! | Goodbye. |
mist: Some languages can drop the subject; in English you always say it.
The 'a' in name sounds like 'ay' /eɪ/.

en-a1-u01-l02.title: The alphabet and spelling
en-a1-u01-l02.objective: By the end you can say the letters of the alphabet and spell your name.
en-a1-u01-l02.warmup: Can you spell your name aloud? In English the letters sound different: let's practise them.
md: **The alphabet** (with IPA):

A /eɪ/ · B /biː/ · C /siː/ · D /diː/ · E /iː/ · F /ef/ · G /dʒiː/ · H /eɪtʃ/ · I /aɪ/ · J /dʒeɪ/ · K /keɪ/ · L /el/ · M /em/ · N /en/ · O /əʊ/ · P /piː/ · Q /kjuː/ · R /ɑː/ · S /es/ · T /tiː/ · U /juː/ · V /viː/ · W /ˈdʌbljuː/ · X /eks/ · Y /waɪ/ · Z /zed/
In British English Z is *zed*; in American English, *zee*.
**Letters people mix up:** E / I, G / J, A / H.
**double** + letter = two identical letters: *Anna* = A, double N, A.
mist: English E sounds like 'ee' and I sounds like 'eye'.
G and J are easy to confuse: practise them together.

en-a1-u01-l03.title: Numbers 0–20 and phone numbers
en-a1-u01-l03.objective: By the end you can count from 0 to 20 and give your phone number.
en-a1-u01-l03.warmup: How do you say your phone number: in groups or digit by digit?
md: | 0 zero | 1 one | 2 two | 3 three | 4 four | 5 five | 6 six |
| 7 seven | 8 eight | 9 nine | 10 ten | 11 eleven | 12 twelve | 13 thirteen |
| 14 fourteen | 15 fifteen | 16 sixteen | 17 seventeen | 18 eighteen | 19 nineteen | 20 twenty |
**Phone numbers:** say them digit by digit. 0 is often said *oh* (also *zero*).
**13–19** end in *-teen* and are stressed on *teen* (thir-TEEN). Later you will see 30, 40… (*-ty*), stressed at the start (THIR-ty).
mist: It ends in a V sound: touch your top teeth to your bottom lip.
In -teen the stress is at the end; in -ty, at the start.

en-a1-u01-l04.title: How are you? Greetings through the day
en-a1-u01-l04.objective: By the end you can greet people according to the time of day, ask how someone is and answer.
en-a1-u01-l04.warmup: What do you say in the morning, the afternoon and the evening in your language? It changes in English too.
md: | Time | Greeting |
| Morning (until noon) | Good morning |
| Afternoon (noon – about 6 pm) | Good afternoon |
| Evening, when you arrive | Good evening |
| When leaving or going to bed | Good night |
**How are you?** is a greeting. Answer: *I'm fine, thanks. And you?* (also *great* or *not bad*).
It's polite to return the question with **And you?**
mist: 'Good night' is only used to say goodbye or before going to bed.
It's polite to return the question.

en-a1-u01-l05.title: How old are you?
en-a1-u01-l05.objective: By the end you can ask and say someone's age, and you know I am / you are.
en-a1-u01-l05.warmup: Which verb does your language use for age? Guess which one English uses.
md: **Age uses *to be*, not *have*:** *I'm 20* (literally 'I am 20').
| Subject | to be | Short form |
| I | am | I'm |
| you | are | you're |
**Question:** *How old are you?* **Answer:** *I'm 20.* or *I'm 20 years old.*
Compound numbers: *twenty-one, twenty-two… twenty-nine*. You will see all the numbers in Unit 8.
mist: Age is expressed with 'to be', not with 'have'.
That literal translation is not used in English.

en-a1-u01-l06.title: Review and checkpoint 1
en-a1-u01-l06.objective: By the end you show that you can introduce yourself, spell, use numbers and greet people in English.
en-a1-u01-l06.warmup: Last step of the unit: test everything you have learnt.
en-a1-u01-l06.recap: Review: greetings (Hello, Good morning…), I'm / My name is, the alphabet, numbers 0–20, How are you? and How old are you?
md: **Quick review**
- Greetings: *Hello / Hi · Good morning / afternoon / evening · Goodbye*
- Introducing yourself: *I'm … / My name is …* and *Nice to meet you.*
- Spelling: *How do you spell …?*
- Numbers 0–20 and phone numbers (digit by digit)
- Age: *I'm 20.* (with *to be*)

en-a1-u02-l01.title: Countries and nationalities
en-a1-u02-l01.objective: By the end you can say which country you are from and your nationality, and ask other people.
en-a1-u02-l01.warmup: Where are you from? Think how you would say it in English with what you know about I'm.
md: **Where are you from?** → *I'm from + country.*
**Nationality:** *I'm + nationality.*
| Country | Nationality |
| Argentina | Argentinian |
| Spain | Spanish |
| Brazil | Brazilian |
| Mexico | Mexican |
| England | English |
| Italy | Italian |
| France | French |
**Capital letters:** in English, countries, nationalities and languages always start with a capital letter. Many nationalities (Spanish, English, French, Italian…) are also the name of the language.
mist: In English, countries and nationalities take a capital letter.
Use 'from', not 'of'.

en-a1-u02-l02.title: He, she, it: the verb to be
en-a1-u02-l02.objective: By the end you can talk about another person or thing with he, she and it.
en-a1-u02-l02.warmup: Look at a photo of some friends: how would you say 'he is from…' and 'she is from…'?
md: | Subject | to be | Short form |
| he | is | he's |
| she | is | she's |
| it | is | it's |
- **he** = a man · **she** = a woman · **it** = a thing or an animal.
- The subject is never dropped: *He's a teacher.* (not *Is a teacher*).
mist: The subject is not dropped.
he = a man, she = a woman.

en-a1-u02-l03.title: We, you, they: the full verb to be
en-a1-u02-l03.objective: By the end you can use all the forms of to be with we, you and they.
en-a1-u02-l03.warmup: You already know I, you, he, she, it. How would you say 'we are' and 'they are'?
md: | Subject | to be | Short form |
| I | am | I'm |
| you | are | you're |
| he / she / it | is | he's / she's / it's |
| we | are | we're |
| you | are | you're |
| they | are | they're |
**you** is used for one person or for several: English has no separate plural 'you'.
Pronunciation: *we're* /wɪə/ · *you're* /jɔː/ · *they're* /ðeə/.
mist: 'they' goes with 'are'.
In English 'you' is used for one person or for several.

en-a1-u02-l04.title: Negatives, questions and short answers
en-a1-u02-l04.objective: By the end you can make negatives and questions with to be, and reply with short answers.
en-a1-u02-l04.warmup: Think: how do you ask 'are you Spanish?' and answer 'no, I'm not'?
en-a1-u02-l04.topic: To be: negatives, questions and short answers
md: **Negative:** to be + **not** → *I'm not · you aren't · he isn't · she isn't · it isn't · we aren't · they aren't*.
**Question:** swap the order → *Are you…? Is she…? Are they…?*
**Short answers:** *Yes, I am. / No, I'm not. · Yes, he is. / No, he isn't. · Yes, we are. / No, we aren't.*
In **affirmative** short answers **don't contract**: *Yes, I am* (not *Yes, I'm*).
mist: Affirmative short answers are not contracted.
In questions the verb comes before the subject.

en-a1-u02-l05.title: Jobs and a / an
en-a1-u02-l05.objective: By the end you can ask about jobs and say yours using a / an.
en-a1-u02-l05.warmup: Some languages say 'I am doctor' with no article. Do you think English needs one?
md: **What do you do?** = What is your job? Answer: *I'm a / an + job.*
**a** before a consonant sound: *a teacher, a nurse*.
**an** before a vowel sound: *an engineer*.
What matters is the **sound**, not the letter: *a university* (starts with a /j/ sound), *an hour* (the h is silent).
With jobs the article is required: *I'm a doctor*, never *I'm doctor*.
mist: With jobs the article is required in English.
Use 'an' before a vowel sound.

en-a1-u02-l06.title: Review and checkpoint 2
en-a1-u02-l06.objective: By the end you show that you can talk about origin, nationality and jobs with to be.
en-a1-u02-l06.warmup: End of the unit: use to be, countries and jobs in real situations.
en-a1-u02-l06.recap: Review: Where are you from?, nationalities, he/she/it/we/they, negatives and questions with to be, and a/an with jobs.
md: **Quick review**
- *Where are you from? I'm from …* · *I'm + nationality*
- *he's / she's / it's · we're / you're / they're*
- *I'm not · he isn't · they aren't* · *Are you…? Yes, I am.*
- *What do you do? I'm a / an …*

en-a1-u03-l01.title: Family members
en-a1-u03-l01.objective: By the end you can name the members of your family and introduce someone in a photo.
en-a1-u03-l01.warmup: Think of a family photo: how would you say 'this is my mother' in English?
md: **Family:** mother (mum) · father (dad) · brother · sister · son · daughter · husband · wife · grandmother · grandfather · parents.
**mum** is British English; in American English it's *mom*.
**Plural:** add *-s*: *brother → brothers*, *sister → sisters*.
**Careful:** *parents* = mother and father only. Other family members are *relatives*.
mist: With more than one, add -s.
parents = mother and father; other family members are relatives.

en-a1-u03-l02.title: Possessive adjectives
en-a1-u03-l02.objective: By the end you can use my, your, his, her, our and their to say who something belongs to.
en-a1-u03-l02.warmup: In some languages one word means 'his', 'her' and 'their'. How does English tell them apart?
en-a1-u03-l02.topic: Possessive adjectives: my, your, his, her, our, their
md: | Subject | Possessive |
| I | my |
| you | your |
| he | his |
| she | her |
| it | its |
| we | our |
| they | their |
**Key rule:** the possessive depends on **who the owner is**, not on the thing: *Tom's sister* → *his sister*; *Anna's brother* → *her brother*.
Possessives **don't change** in the plural: *my brothers*.
mist: Use the possessive (her), not the pronoun (she).
Possessives don't change in the plural.

en-a1-u03-l03.title: The possessive 's
en-a1-u03-l03.objective: By the end you can say 'Anna's brother' with the possessive 's.
en-a1-u03-l03.warmup: English puts the owner first: how do you think 'the brother of Anna' sounds in English?
md: **Possession:** *owner + 's + thing/person* → *Anna's brother*.
The **owner comes first**.
**Careful:** *'s* can also be *is*: *Sue's a nurse* (Sue **is**…) vs *Sue's brother* (the brother **of** Sue).
mist: In English the owner comes first, with 's.
Don't forget the apostrophe.

en-a1-u03-l04.title: Have got
en-a1-u03-l04.objective: By the end you can talk about what you have (brothers, family) with have got.
en-a1-u03-l04.warmup: You can already say 'I am' and 'it is'. How would you say 'I have a brother' in British English?
md: **Have got** = have (British English).
| Subject | Affirmative | Negative |
| I / you / we / they | have got (I've got) | haven't got |
| he / she / it | has got (she's got) | hasn't got |
**Question:** *Have you got…? Has she got…?* **Answer:** *Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.*
American English uses *I have* and *Do you have…?* more; both are understood. *'s got* = *has got*, not *is*.
mist: With he/she/it use has.
Affirmative short answers are not contracted.

en-a1-u03-l05.title: Describing people
en-a1-u03-l05.objective: By the end you can describe people with adjectives and put them in the right place.
en-a1-u03-l05.warmup: What is someone in your family like? Think about where adjectives go in English: before or after the noun?
md: **Adjectives don't change** for gender or number: *a tall man, a tall woman, tall people*.
**Position:**
- after *to be*: *She is tall.*
- **before** the noun: *a tall woman* (never *a woman tall*).
No *-s* is added: *They are tall* (not *talls*).
mist: In English the adjective goes before the noun.
Adjectives don't change in the plural.

en-a1-u03-l06.title: Review and checkpoint 3
en-a1-u03-l06.objective: By the end you show that you can talk about and describe your family in English.
en-a1-u03-l06.warmup: End of the unit: introduce your family with everything you have learnt.
en-a1-u03-l06.recap: Review: family members, possessives (my, his, her…), 's, have got and adjectives to describe people.
md: **Quick review**
- *This is my mother / father / brother…*
- *my · your · his · her · our · their*
- *Anna's brother* (owner + 's)
- *I've got … · She's got … · Have you got any …?*
- *a tall woman · They are tall*

en-a1-u04-l01.title: Daily activities
en-a1-u04-l01.objective: By the end you can name the activities of a normal day and say when you do them.
en-a1-u04-l01.warmup: Think about your day: what is the first thing you do when you wake up and the last thing before bed?
md: **Routine verbs** (most use *have* or *go*):
- *have breakfast / lunch / dinner* (not *take breakfast*)
- *go to work / school / bed* · *go home* (no *to*)
- *get up, watch TV*
**Times of day:** *in the morning · in the afternoon · in the evening · at night*.
mist: Meals go with 'have'.
With 'home' you don't use 'to'.

en-a1-u04-l02.title: What time is it?
en-a1-u04-l02.objective: By the end you can ask and tell the time, and say what time things happen.
en-a1-u04-l02.warmup: How do you ask the time in your language? Now let's see how it's done in English.
md: **Asking:** *What time is it?* · *What time is the class?*
**Answering:** *It's + time.*
| Time | You say |
| 8:00 | It's eight o'clock. |
| 8:10 | It's ten past eight. |
| 8:15 | It's quarter past eight. |
| 8:20 | It's twenty past eight. |
| 8:30 | It's half past eight. |
| 8:40 | It's twenty to nine. |
| 8:45 | It's quarter to nine. |
- Up to half past, use **past**; after half past, use **to** (the next hour).
- You can also say it like a digital clock: *eight forty*.
- For events: **at** + time → *at nine o'clock*.
mist: There is no article before the time in English.
Always 'it is', even with several hours.

en-a1-u04-l03.title: Present simple: affirmative
en-a1-u04-l03.objective: By the end you can describe routines with the present simple, including the -s form for he / she / it.
en-a1-u04-l03.warmup: Look at the text: what happens to the verb when we talk about Lucy and not about ourselves?
md: **Present simple** = habits and routines.
- **I / you / we / they** → base verb: *I work, they work*.
- **he / she / it** → verb + **-s**: *she works, he gets up*.
| Verb ending | Change | Example |
| normal | + s | works, gets |
| -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o | + es | finishes, watches, goes |
| have | has (irregular) | she has |
Pronunciation of -s: /s/ (works), /z/ (gets… *plays*), /ɪz/ (watches, finishes).
mist: With he/she/it the verb takes -s.
Have is irregular: has.

en-a1-u04-l04.title: Present simple: negatives and questions
en-a1-u04-l04.objective: By the end you can make negatives and questions in the present simple with do / does.
en-a1-u04-l04.warmup: With to be we swapped the verb. Other verbs need a helper: which one do you think it is?
en-a1-u04-l04.topic: Present simple: negatives, questions and short answers
md: **Negative:** subject + **don't / doesn't** + base verb.
*I don't work. She doesn't work.*
**Question:** **Do / Does** + subject + base verb.
*Do you work? Does she work?*
**Short answers:** *Yes, I do. / No, I don't. · Yes, she does. / No, she doesn't.*
**With Wh- questions:** *What time do you get up?*
After *does / doesn't* the verb **takes no -s**: *She doesn't work* (not *works*).
mist: With does/doesn't the verb takes no -s.
The negative is formed with don't, not with 'no'.

en-a1-u04-l05.title: Days of the week and frequency
en-a1-u04-l05.objective: By the end you can say the days of the week and how often you do things.
en-a1-u04-l05.warmup: How many times a week do you exercise? English has words for that frequency.
en-a1-u04-l05.topic: Adverbs of frequency and days of the week
md: **Days:** Monday · Tuesday · Wednesday · Thursday · Friday · Saturday · Sunday. Always with a **capital letter**.
**on + day:** *on Monday(s)* (no article).
| Adverb | Frequency |
| always | 100 % |
| usually | ~80 % |
| often | ~60 % |
| sometimes | ~30 % |
| never | 0 % |
**Position:** before the main verb (*She always gets up*) and after *to be* (*She is always late*).
mist: The adverb goes before the main verb.
Days take a capital letter and no article.

en-a1-u04-l06.title: Review and checkpoint 4
en-a1-u04-l06.objective: By the end you show that you can describe your routine, tell the time and ask about habits.
en-a1-u04-l06.warmup: End of the unit: describe your whole day.
en-a1-u04-l06.recap: Review: daily activities, the time, present simple (-s / -es), negatives and questions with do / does, days and adverbs of frequency.
md: **Quick review**
- *get up, have breakfast, go to work, go to bed*
- *It's half past eight · quarter to nine*
- *I work · she works · he goes · she has*
- *I don't work · She doesn't work · Do you work? Does he work?*
- *on Mondays · always · usually · sometimes · never*

en-a1-u05-l01.title: Food and drink
en-a1-u05-l01.objective: By the end you can name common food and drinks and pronounce them well.
en-a1-u05-l01.warmup: What did you have for breakfast today? Let's see how common food and drinks are said in English.
md: **Food:** bread · rice · egg · cheese · chicken · fish · apple · banana · salad · pasta · sandwich
**Drinks:** milk · water · coffee · tea · juice
**Verbs:** *eat*, *drink*, *have* (*have a coffee*).
Pronunciation: *cheese* ends in /z/ · *juice* is /dʒuːs/ · *banana* is stressed on the second syllable (ba-NA-na).
mist: It sounds like 'joos' /dʒuːs/.
It ends in /z/ and the vowel is long.

en-a1-u05-l02.title: Plurals
en-a1-u05-l02.objective: By the end you can form regular and irregular plurals.
en-a1-u05-l02.warmup: One egg, two eggs: how does the word change in English when there is more than one?
md: **Regular plural:** + **s** → *apple → apples, banana → bananas*.
**+ es** after *-s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o*: *sandwich → sandwiches, tomato → tomatoes, potato → potatoes*.
**Consonant + y → -ies:** *strawberry → strawberries*.
**Irregular:** man → men · woman → women · child → children · person → people · foot → feet.
Pronunciation of -s: /s/ (cats), /z/ (bananas), /ɪz/ (sandwiches).
mist: After -ch add -es.
These are irregular plurals.

en-a1-u05-l03.title: Likes: like, love, hate
en-a1-u05-l03.objective: By the end you can say what you like and what you don't like with like, love and hate.
en-a1-u05-l03.warmup: In English the person who likes something is the subject: how do you think 'I like fish' works?
md: **like + noun:** *I like fish. I like apples.* (no article when speaking in general)
The subject is **the person** who has the feeling: *I like fish* (I + like + fish).
**Scale:** love > like > don't like > hate.
**With he/she/it:** *She likes tea.* · *He doesn't like coffee.*
**Question:** *Do you like fish? — Yes, I do. / No, I don't.* · *What's your favourite food?*
mist: The subject is the person who feels: I.
With he/she/it the verb takes -s.

en-a1-u05-l04.title: Meals: some and any
en-a1-u05-l04.objective: By the end you can name the meals of the day and use some and any.
en-a1-u05-l04.warmup: Have we got any milk? Is there any bread? Let's see how to say 'some' and 'no / not any' in English.
md: **some** → **affirmative** sentences: *I've got some bread.*
**any** → **negatives and questions**: *We haven't got any milk. Have we got any bread?*
They are used with plurals (*some apples*) and with things you can't count (*some milk*).
**Useful exception:** in offers and requests use *some*: *Would you like some tea?*
**Meals:** breakfast · lunch · dinner (*for breakfast*).
mist: In negatives use any.
In affirmative sentences use some.

en-a1-u05-l05.title: At the café: ordering and paying
en-a1-u05-l05.objective: By the end you can politely order food and drink in a café and ask the price.
en-a1-u05-l05.warmup: In a café, how do you ask for something politely in your language? English has some very useful set phrases.
en-a1-u05-l05.topic: Ordering politely: I'd like / Can I have...?
md: **Ordering:** *I'd like a coffee, please.* or *Can I have a coffee, please?*
**I'd like** = *I would like*. It's more polite than *I want*, which sounds abrupt.
**Always with *please*.**
**Waiter:** *What would you like? · Anything else?*
**Paying:** *Here you are.* · *That's six pounds.* · *Thank you!*
mist: I want sounds abrupt when ordering.
Give me is an order; it's better to ask with Can I have…?

en-a1-u05-l06.title: Review and checkpoint 5
en-a1-u05-l06.objective: By the end you show that you can talk about food and likes and order in a café.
en-a1-u05-l06.warmup: End of the unit: use everything in real situations.
en-a1-u05-l06.recap: Review: food and drinks, plurals, like / love / hate, some and any, and ordering with I'd like / Can I have…?
md: **Quick review**
- *bread, cheese, chicken, milk, juice…*
- *tomato → tomatoes · child → children*
- *I like / love / hate … · She likes … · She doesn't like …*
- *some* (affirmative) / *any* (negatives and questions)
- *I'd like …, please. · Can I have …, please?*

en-a1-u06-l01.title: Rooms and furniture
en-a1-u06-l01.objective: By the end you can name the rooms and furniture of a home and show your home.
en-a1-u06-l01.warmup: Imagine a friend visits your home for the first time: what do you show them?
md: **Rooms:** kitchen · living room · bedroom · bathroom · garden
**Furniture and objects:** bed · table · chair · sofa · lamp · window · door
**house** and **flat** (British English; in American English it's *apartment*).
**Careful:** *toilet* is the toilet itself or a WC; *bathroom* is the room in a home.
Pronunciation: *sofa* → 'SOH-fa' · *kitchen* → 'KIT-chen' · *chair* → 'chair'.
mist: bathroom = room; toilet = the toilet itself. They're different things.
The first vowel sounds 'oh'.

en-a1-u06-l02.title: There is / There are
en-a1-u06-l02.objective: By the end you can say what there is (and isn't) in a place with there is and there are.
en-a1-u06-l02.warmup: Many languages use one word for 'there is/are'. How does English tell one from many?
md: **There is** (there's) + singular → *There's a sofa.*
**There are** + plural → *There are two chairs.*
| | Singular | Plural |
| + | There is a lamp. | There are two lamps. |
| − | There isn't a lamp. | There aren't any lamps. |
| ? | Is there a lamp? | Are there any lamps? |
**Short answers:** *Yes, there is. / No, there isn't. · Yes, there are. / No, there aren't.*
**Don't leave out there** and **don't use *have***: *There are two bedrooms* (not *Have two bedrooms*).
mist: To say something exists use there is / there are, not have.
With a plural use there are.

en-a1-u06-l03.title: Prepositions of place
en-a1-u06-l03.objective: By the end you can say where things are with prepositions of place.
en-a1-u06-l03.warmup: Where did you leave your keys? Say it in English: on, under, next to…
md: **in** (inside) · **on** (on top, touching) · **under** (below) · **next to** (beside) · **behind** · **in front of** · **between** (two things)
**Question:** *Where's my phone?* (= Where is) · *Where are my keys?*
Careful: *on the table* (not *in the table*) and *next to* needs **to**.
mist: On a surface use 'on'.
Don't forget 'to' or 'of'.

en-a1-u06-l04.title: Colours and adjectives
en-a1-u06-l04.objective: By the end you can name colours and describe objects with adjectives in the right order.
en-a1-u06-l04.warmup: What colour is your room? Learn the colours and where they go in the sentence.
md: **Colours:** red · blue · green · yellow · black · white · brown · grey · pink · orange
**The adjective goes before the noun** and doesn't change: *a red lamp, two red lamps* (not *a lamp red*, not *reds lamps*).
With *to be* it goes after: *The lamp is red.*
*grey* (British) = *gray* (American) · *colour* (British) = *color* (American).
mist: The adjective goes before the noun.
Adjectives don't change in the plural.

en-a1-u06-l05.title: Describe your home
en-a1-u06-l05.objective: By the end you can describe where you live and what your home is like in 4 or 5 sentences.
en-a1-u06-l05.warmup: Tell someone new where you live and what your home is like. Bring together everything from the unit.
md: **Where you live:** *I live in + city* (no article): *I live in Buenos Aires.* · *I live in a flat / a house.*
**How many rooms:** *There are three rooms.*
**What they're like:** *The sofa is grey. The kitchen is small.*
**Question:** *Where do you live?*
**A tip:** join sentences with *and* and *but*.
mist: Cities don't take an article.
With houses and flats use 'in'.

en-a1-u06-l06.title: Review and checkpoint 6
en-a1-u06-l06.objective: By the end you show that you can name parts of a home, say what there is and where it is.
en-a1-u06-l06.warmup: End of the unit: describe a whole room.
en-a1-u06-l06.recap: Review: rooms and furniture, there is / there are, prepositions of place, colours and describing your home.
md: **Quick review**
- *kitchen, bedroom, bathroom, sofa, lamp, window*
- *There's a … / There are two … / Is there a …?*
- *in · on · under · next to · behind · in front of · between*
- *a red lamp · The sofa is blue.*
- *I live in a flat in …*

en-a1-u07-l01.title: Places in town
en-a1-u07-l01.objective: By the end you can name the main places in a town and say what is nearby.
en-a1-u07-l01.warmup: What places are there in your neighbourhood? Learn how to say them in English.
md: **Places:** bank · supermarket · restaurant · café · hospital · school · park · station · post office · cinema · library · museum
**library** is where you borrow books; a shop that sells books is a *bookshop* (*bookstore* in American English).
**There's…:** *There's a park near my house.*
Pronunciation: *museum* → myoo-ZEE-um · *library* → LIE-bruh-ree · *station* → STAY-shn.
mist: library = a place to borrow books; bookshop = a place to buy them.
It sounds 'myoo-ZEE-um', stressed on the second syllable.

en-a1-u07-l02.title: Where is...?
en-a1-u07-l02.objective: By the end you can ask where a place is and answer with prepositions and distances.
en-a1-u07-l02.warmup: You're in a new city looking for a bank: how do you ask where it is?
md: **Asking:** *Where's the bank?* (= *Where is…*) · *Is there a bank near here?*
**Answering:** *It's + preposition + place* → *It's next to the supermarket.*
New place words: **opposite** (facing), **near** (close to), **far from** (a long way from).
**Far / near:** *Is it far? — No, it's near.*
Don't leave out the subject: *It's next to…* (not *Is next to…*).
mist: In questions the verb goes before the subject.
In English the subject can't be left out.

en-a1-u07-l03.title: Getting there: directions
en-a1-u07-l03.objective: By the end you can ask for and give directions to a place.
en-a1-u07-l03.warmup: A tourist asks you how to get to the station. What do you say?
md: **Asking:** *How do I get to the station?*
**Giving directions (imperative):**
- *Go straight on.* (keep going ahead)
- *Turn left / right.*
- *Take the first / second / third left / right.* (the first, second… street on the left / right)
- *at the traffic lights / at the corner*
**Location:** *It's on your left / on your right.* (with **on**, not *in*).
mist: Don't use 'to' with left / right.
Left / right position goes with 'on'.

en-a1-u07-l04.title: Transport
en-a1-u07-l04.objective: By the end you can say how you get to places with by and on foot.
en-a1-u07-l04.warmup: How do you get to work or school? Learn how to say it in English.
md: **by + transport** (no article): *by bus · by train · by car · by taxi · by bike · by underground*.
**Walking:** *on foot* or *walk*: *I go to school on foot.* = *I walk to school.*
**Question:** *How do you go to work?*
You don't say *by the bus* or *by foot*.
Pronunciation: *walk* → 'wok' (the l is silent).
mist: With by, don't use an article.
Walking is 'on foot'.

en-a1-u07-l05.title: Imperatives and polite requests
en-a1-u07-l05.objective: By the end you can give instructions and polite requests with the imperative and ask for help.
en-a1-u07-l05.warmup: How do you get a stranger's attention to ask for help in the street?
md: **Imperative** = base form of the verb, **no subject**: *Turn left. Wait here. Stop.*
**Negative:** **Don't** + verb → *Don't turn left. Don't run.*
**More polite:** add *please* → *Please wait here.* or use *Can you…?* → *Can you help me, please?*
**Excuse me** = to get attention or get past. **Sorry** = to apologise.
mist: The negative imperative uses Don't.
The imperative has no subject.

en-a1-u07-l06.title: Review and checkpoint 7
en-a1-u07-l06.objective: By the end you show that you can ask for and give directions and get around a town in English.
en-a1-u07-l06.warmup: End of the unit: help a tourist get to their destination.
en-a1-u07-l06.recap: Review: places in town, Where is…?, directions, transport with by / on foot and the imperative.
md: **Quick review**
- *bank, library, station, post office, cinema*
- *Where's the bank? · It's next to / opposite / near …*
- *How do I get to …? · Go straight on · Turn left · Take the second right*
- *by bus · by car · on foot*
- *Excuse me · Don't turn left · Please wait here*

en-a1-u08-l01.title: Numbers 21 to 1000
en-a1-u08-l01.objective: By the end you can count from 21 to 1000 and ask how many there are with how many.
en-a1-u08-l01.warmup: You can already count to twenty. How would you say thirty-five, ninety or a hundred and fifty?
md: | 20 twenty | 30 thirty | 40 forty | 50 fifty |
| 60 sixty | 70 seventy | 80 eighty | 90 ninety |
**Compounds:** ten + unit with a hyphen → *twenty-one, thirty-five, ninety-nine*.
**100 = a / one hundred · 1,000 = a / one thousand.** British English adds *and* after *hundred*: *one hundred and fifty* (150).
**No plural:** *two hundred* (not *two hundreds*).
**Watch the stress:** thir**TEEN** (13) / **THIR**ty (30), fif**TEEN** (15) / **FIF**ty (50).
**Question:** *How many people are in the class?*
mist: Hundred takes no -s after a number.
They differ in stress and ending.

en-a1-u08-l02.title: Prices and money
en-a1-u08-l02.objective: By the end you can ask prices and say amounts of money.
en-a1-u08-l02.warmup: At a market, how do you ask how much something costs? And how do you say the price?
md: **Asking:** *How much is the sandwich?* (singular) · *How much are the bananas?* (plural)
**Answering:** *It's three pounds.* · *They're two pounds fifty.*
**Prices:** £2.50 = *two pounds fifty* (or *two fifty*) · $5.99 = *five ninety-nine*
**Currencies take -s:** *pounds, euros, dollars* (*two pounds*, not *two pound*).
**cheap** = low price · **expensive** = high price.
mist: Use 'is' or 'are', not 'cost'.
The currency takes -s in the plural.

en-a1-u08-l03.title: Clothes
en-a1-u08-l03.objective: By the end you can name clothes and say what you're wearing with wear.
en-a1-u08-l03.warmup: What are you wearing today? Learn how to say each item in English.
md: **Clothes:** shirt · T-shirt · trousers · jeans · dress · skirt · jacket · coat · shoes · socks · hat
**wear** = have clothes on your body: *She wears a dress.* (not *use*)
**Pair plurals:** *trousers, jeans, shoes, socks* are always plural: *My jeans are blue.* For one: *a pair of jeans / trousers / shoes*.
**The colour goes before** the item: *blue jeans, a white T-shirt.*
mist: For clothes use wear.
Trousers, jeans and shoes are plural.

en-a1-u08-l04.title: This, that, these, those
en-a1-u08-l04.objective: By the end you can point to near and far things with this, that, these and those.
en-a1-u08-l04.warmup: Near or far, one or many: English has four words to point at things. Let's see them.
md: | | Singular | Plural |
| **Near** | this | these |
| **Far** | that | those |
**With a noun:** *this jacket, these shoes, that hat, those socks.*
**On their own:** *This is my bag. These are my keys.*
**Agreement:** this/that + singular · these/those + plural: *these shoes* (not *this shoes*).
Pronunciation: *this* /ðɪs/ (short i) vs *these* /ðiːz/ (long i).
mist: With a plural use these.
Far, singular: that.

en-a1-u08-l05.title: In the shop
en-a1-u08-l05.objective: By the end you can buy clothes in a shop: ask, try on and pay.
en-a1-u08-l05.warmup: You're in a clothes shop. What would you say to ask for help, try something on and pay?
en-a1-u08-l05.topic: In the shop: Can I try it on? / I'll take it
md: **Shop assistant:** *Can I help you? · What size are you? · It's forty pounds.*
**Customer:**
- *I'm looking for a jacket.*
- *Can I try it on?*
- *Have you got this in medium?*
- *How much is it?* · *I'll take it.* (= I'm buying it)
- *Can I pay by card / in cash?*
**Sizes:** small · medium · large.
**Just looking:** *I'm just looking, thanks.*
mist: For something happening now use I'm looking for.
When you decide to buy, say I'll take it.

en-a1-u08-l06.title: Review and checkpoint 8
en-a1-u08-l06.objective: By the end you show that you can buy clothes and talk about prices and amounts in English.
en-a1-u08-l06.warmup: End of the unit: buy, pay and ask as in a real shop.
en-a1-u08-l06.recap: Review: numbers 21 to 1000, How much is / are…?, clothes and wear, this / that / these / those, and shop phrases.
md: **Quick review**
- *thirty-five · ninety · one hundred and fifty · one thousand*
- *How much is it? · How much are they? · two pounds fifty*
- *shirt, trousers, jeans, dress · She wears …*
- *this / these (near) · that / those (far)*
- *I'm looking for … · Can I try it on? · I'll take it.*

en-a1-u09-l01.title: Free time and hobbies
en-a1-u09-l01.objective: By the end you can talk about your hobbies and what you do in your free time.
en-a1-u09-l01.warmup: What do you like doing when you're not working or studying? Learn how to say it in English.
md: **With *play*:** sports without an article → *play football, play tennis*. Instruments with *the* → *play the guitar, play the piano*.
**With other verbs:** *read books · watch films · swim · cook · dance · sing · go for a walk*.
**Careful:** *listen **to** music* (always with *to*).
**Question:** *What do you do in your free time?*
Pronunciation: *guitar* → gi-TAR · *music* → MYOO-zik.
mist: Sports don't take an article.
Listen always takes 'to'.

en-a1-u09-l02.title: Abilities: can / can't
en-a1-u09-l02.objective: By the end you can say what you can and can't do with can and can't.
en-a1-u09-l02.warmup: Can you swim? Can you play the guitar? In English you ask with a single word: can.
md: **can** = be able to / know how to (do something). It's the same for every person and **takes no -s**.
| | Example |
| + | I can swim. · She can swim. |
| − | I can't swim. (can't = cannot) |
| ? | Can you swim? |
**Short answers:** *Yes, I can. / No, I can't.*
After *can* use the base verb **without *to***: *I can cook* (not *I can to cook*).
Pronunciation: *can* is weak /kən/; *can't* is strong and long /kɑːnt/.
mist: Can doesn't change or take -s.
Don't use to after can.

en-a1-u09-l03.title: Asking and allowing with can
en-a1-u09-l03.objective: By the end you can ask for permission and ask favours with Can I…? and Can you…?
en-a1-u09-l03.warmup: How do you ask permission to open a window, or ask someone to close the door?
en-a1-u09-l03.topic: Can I...? / Can you...?: asking and allowing
md: **Can I…?** = asking for permission → *Can I open the window?*
**Can you…?** = asking a favour → *Can you close the door?*
**Add *please*** to sound friendlier.
**Answering:** *Yes, of course. / Sure. / Sorry, you can't.*
After *can* use the base verb: *Can you help me?* (not *Can you me help?* or *Can I to open…?*).
mist: The verb goes right after the subject.
Don't use to after can.

en-a1-u09-l04.title: Present continuous
en-a1-u09-l04.objective: By the end you can say what you're doing now with the present continuous.
en-a1-u09-l04.warmup: Someone calls you and asks 'what are you doing?'. How would you answer in English?
md: **Present continuous** = actions happening **now**: *be* + verb + **-ing**.
| + | I'm cooking · she's cooking · they're cooking |
| − | I'm not cooking · he isn't cooking · we aren't cooking |
| ? | Are you cooking? · Is she cooking? |
**Short answers:** *Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.*
**-ing spelling:**
- normal: *work → working*
- ends in -e (drop it): *make → making*
- short vowel + consonant (double it): *swim → swimming, run → running*
**Habit vs now:** *I play football on Saturdays* (always) · *I'm playing football now* (now).
mist: The verb to be is missing.
After be the verb takes -ing.

en-a1-u09-l05.title: Inviting and accepting
en-a1-u09-l05.objective: By the end you can invite someone, accept or say no politely, and suggest plans.
en-a1-u09-l05.warmup: How do you invite a friend to the cinema? And how do you say you can't without sounding rude?
en-a1-u09-l05.topic: Inviting and accepting: Would you like to...? / Let's...
md: **Inviting:**
- *Would you like to + verb…?* → *Would you like to go to the cinema?*
- *Let's + verb* → *Let's meet at seven.* (no *to*)
- *What about + day/plan?* → *What about Saturday?*
**Accepting:** *I'd love to! · Great idea! · Yes, please.*
**Saying no politely:** *Sorry, I can't. I work on Fridays.* (give a reason).
**Time:** *on Friday · at seven.*
mist: After Would you like use to.
Don't use to after Let's.

en-a1-u09-l06.title: Review and checkpoint 9
en-a1-u09-l06.objective: By the end you show that you can talk about hobbies, abilities, requests, things happening now and invitations.
en-a1-u09-l06.warmup: End of the unit: use everything in real conversations.
en-a1-u09-l06.recap: Review: hobbies, can / can't, Can I…? / Can you…?, the present continuous and invitations with Would you like to…?
md: **Quick review**
- *play football · play the guitar · listen to music*
- *I can swim · I can't dance · Can you sing?*
- *Can I open the window? · Can you help me?*
- *I'm cooking · She isn't working · What are you doing?*
- *Would you like to …? · I'd love to · Let's meet at seven.*

en-a1-u10-l01.title: The weather
en-a1-u10-l01.objective: By the end you can describe the weather and ask what it's like somewhere else.
en-a1-u10-l01.warmup: What's the weather like in your city today? Learn to describe it in English.
en-a1-u10-l01.topic: Talking about the weather: It's sunny / It's raining
md: **Asking:** *What's the weather like in London?*
**Answering:** *It's + adjective* → *It's sunny / cloudy / windy / hot / warm / cold.*
**For rain and snow** use the present continuous: *It's raining. It's snowing.*
**It is compulsory**, even though it doesn't refer to anything: *It's cold* (not *Is cold*).
**Careful:** *It's cold* (the weather) ≠ *I'm cold* (you feel cold). *I have a cold* means 'I'm ill with a cold'.
mist: The subject it is compulsory.
'I'm cold' = I feel cold; 'a cold' = an illness.

en-a1-u10-l02.title: Months and seasons
en-a1-u10-l02.objective: By the end you can name the months and seasons and say when things happen with in.
en-a1-u10-l02.warmup: In which month does summer start where you live? Learn the months and seasons in English.
md: **Months:** January · February · March · April · May · June · July · August · September · October · November · December. Always with a **capital letter**.
**Seasons:** spring · summer · autumn (*fall* in American English) · winter. Lower case.
**in + month / season:** *in January · in summer.*
**Careful:** the southern hemisphere has the seasons the other way round: summer in Argentina is December–February; in the UK it's June–August.
mist: Months take a capital letter.
With months and seasons use in.

en-a1-u10-l03.title: Dates and ordinals
en-a1-u10-l03.objective: By the end you can use ordinal numbers to say and ask about dates and birthdays.
en-a1-u10-l03.warmup: When's your birthday? In English, days of the month are said with ordinal numbers (first, second…).
md: **Ordinals:** 1st first · 2nd second · 3rd third · 4th fourth · 5th **fifth** · 6th sixth · 7th seventh · 8th **eighth** · 9th **ninth** · 10th tenth · 12th **twelfth** · 20th twentieth · 21st twenty-first
**Rule:** number + **-th**, except 1st, 2nd and 3rd. Watch the changes: *five → fifth, eight → eighth, nine → ninth, twelve → twelfth*.
**Dates (British English):** *the fifth of May* (5 May). Written *5th May* or *5 May*. American English: *May fifth*.
**Preposition:** *on the fifth of May* · *in May*.
**Asking:** *What's the date today? · When's your birthday?*
mist: The day is an ordinal number.
With a specific day use on.

en-a1-u10-l04.title: Plans with the present continuous
en-a1-u10-l04.objective: By the end you can talk about your plans with the present continuous and a future time expression.
en-a1-u10-l04.warmup: For plans that are already arranged, English uses -ing with a time word: I'm going to the cinema tomorrow.
md: **Plans already decided:** present continuous + future time word → *I'm meeting Anna on Saturday.*
**Time words:** *tomorrow · this weekend · next week · on Saturday · at eight*.
**Question:** *What are you doing this weekend?*
**Compare:** *I'm cooking now.* (now) · *I'm cooking tomorrow.* (future plan). Without a time word, it means 'now'.
Don't use the present simple for arranged plans; use **-ing**: *I'm going to the cinema tomorrow*.
mist: Plans are expressed with the present continuous.
After be the verb takes -ing.

en-a1-u10-l05.title: Putting it together: a weekend away
en-a1-u10-l05.objective: By the end you can describe a complete weekend plan: where you're going, how you're travelling, where you're staying and what the weather is like.
en-a1-u10-l05.warmup: Bring together everything you've learned to describe a weekend trip.
md: **How to tell a plan:**
1. Where: *We're going to Brighton.*
2. When: *next weekend · on Saturday · at nine o'clock.*
3. How: *We're taking the train.*
4. Where you stay: *We're staying in a small hotel.*
5. Weather: *It's sunny and warm.*
**Prepositions of time:** *on Saturday · in the morning / evening · at nine · in June.*
**No article:** *next weekend* (not *the next weekend*).
mist: Next takes no article in time expressions.
With days use on.

en-a1-u10-l06.title: Review and checkpoint 10
en-a1-u10-l06.objective: By the end you show A1 level: introducing yourself and talking about your daily life, surroundings, likes and plans.
en-a1-u10-l06.warmup: Last A1 checkpoint: bring together everything you've learned.
en-a1-u10-l06.recap: Unit 10 review: to be, possessives and have got, present simple, there is / are, can, present continuous, prices, dates, weather and plans.
md: **Unit 10 review**
- *I'm / She's from … · Where are you from?*
- *my / his / her · Anna's brother · I've got …*
- *I get up · She works · Do you like …? · I don't work*
- *There is / are · in · on · next to · Turn left*
- *How much is it? · these / those · I'd like …, please.*
- *I can swim · Can I …? · I'm cooking · Would you like to …?*
- *It's cold · the fifth of May · I'm going to … tomorrow.*

en-a1-u11-l01.title: Everyday objects
en-a1-u11-l01.objective: By the end you can name the things you carry and use every day: book, pen, keys, phone, wallet…
en-a1-u11-l01.warmup: Look at what's near you now: a phone, some keys, a pen. How do you say them in English?
md: **Everyday objects**
| For writing and studying | Electronics | Personal |
| book · pen · pencil · notebook | phone · computer · camera · headphones | keys · wallet · glasses · watch · umbrella · bag |
**Singular and plural:** *a pen → two pens · a key → keys · a bag → bags*.
**Always plural:** *glasses, headphones, keys* (usually) and *trousers*. You say **My glasses are on the table** (with *are*). For one: *a pair of glasses*.
**a / an:** *a pen, a notebook* · *an umbrella, an apple* (it depends on the **sound**: vowel → an).
**watch vs clock:** *watch* = a clock you wear on your wrist (also the verb 'look at'); *clock* = on a wall or table.
**Careful:** *carpet* covers the floor; a cover for papers is a *folder*.
Pronunciation: *pencil* /ˈpensl/ · *computer* /kəmˈpjuːtə/ · *umbrella* /ʌmˈbrelə/ · *wallet* /ˈwɒlɪt/.
mist: Glasses is plural.
Umbrella starts with a vowel sound: an.

en-a1-u11-l02.title: What's this? Singular and plural
en-a1-u11-l02.objective: By the end you can ask and say what an object is with What's this?, What are these? and Is this your…?
en-a1-u11-l02.warmup: Someone shows you an object you don't know: how do you ask what it is and how do you answer?
en-a1-u11-l02.topic: What's this? / What are these? and Is this your…?
md: **Singular**
- **What's this / that?** → **It's a / an** + object. *What's this? — It's a camera.*
- **Is this / that your …?** → *Yes, it is.* / *No, it isn't.*
**Plural**
- **What are these / those?** → **They're** + plural object. *What are these? — They're headphones.*
- **Are these / those your …?** → *Yes, they are.* / *No, they aren't.*
| | Near | Far |
| Singular | this | that |
| Plural | these | those |
**Plurals:** *-s* (pens) · *-es* after s, sh, ch, x (glasses, watches, boxes) · *-ies* (baby → babies).
**Useful question:** *How do you spell it?* → spell it letter by letter (the alphabet from unit 1).
Careful: *What's this? — It's a camera* (not *This is a camera* as the answer). *Headphones* is plural: *They're headphones.*
Pronunciation: *what's* /wɒts/ · *they're* /ðeə/ · *these* /ðiːz/.
mist: With a plural use are.
Glasses is plural.

en-a1-u11-l03.title: Articles: a, an, the and when to use them
en-a1-u11-l03.objective: By the end you can choose between a, an, the and no article depending on whether something is new, known or general.
en-a1-u11-l03.warmup: 'I've got a dog. The dog is called Max.' The article changes, and English has very clear rules for it.
en-a1-u11-l03.topic: Articles: a, an, the and no article
md: **a / an → something new or any one (singular countable)**
*I've got **a** dog.* · *She's **an** engineer.* (an + vowel sound: *an hour, a university*)
**the → something already mentioned, known to everyone or unique**
*I've got a dog. **The** dog is called Max.* · ***The** sun is hot.* · *Open **the** door, please.*
**No article (∅)**
- **Plurals and uncountables in general:** *I like animals. · I like music. · I love pizza.*
- **Meals:** *I have breakfast at eight.* · **Routines:** *I go to school / work / bed / home. · I'm at home.*
- **Names of people, cities and countries:** *I live in London.* (with some exceptions: *the UK, the USA*).
**Summary:** first time → **a / an**; second time or specific → **the**; in general → **nothing**.
**Pronouncing *the*:** /ðə/ before a consonant sound (*the book*) and /ðiː/ before a vowel sound (*the apple*).
Careful: don't say *I'm teacher* (jobs need an article: *I'm a teacher*) or *the breakfast* for the usual meal.
mist: Jobs need a / an.
No article with meals.

en-a1-u11-l04.title: Where's my...? Objects and places
en-a1-u11-l04.objective: By the end you can ask and say where something is with Where's…? / Where are…? and prepositions of place.
en-a1-u11-l04.warmup: 'I can't find my keys.' Let's ask about lost objects and say exactly where they are.
en-a1-u11-l04.topic: Asking and saying where objects are
md: **Asking about an object**
- **Where's** (is) + singular? → *Where's my phone?* — **It's** + place.
- **Where are** + plural? → *Where are my keys?* — **They're** + place.
- **Is it / Are they** + place? → *Are they on the table? — Yes, they are. / No, they aren't.*
- **I can't find** my … · **Look in / on** …
**Prepositions of place:** *in* (inside) · *on* (on top of) · *under* (below) · *next to* (beside) · *in front of* · *behind* · *between* · *near* (close to).
| Sentence | Meaning |
| It's **in** the bag. | Inside the bag. |
| It's **on** the table. | On top of the table. |
| It's **under** the sofa. | Below the sofa. |
| It's **between** the lamp and the window. | With the lamp on one side and the window on the other. |
Careful: *Where is my glasses?* ✗ → *Where are my glasses?* ✓ (glasses is plural). *In front **of*** needs *of*.
Pronunciation: *behind* /bɪˈhaɪnd/ · *between* /bɪˈtwiːn/ · *pocket* /ˈpɒkɪt/.
mist: Keys is plural.
In front of.

en-a1-u11-l05.title: Instructions and short messages
en-a1-u11-l05.objective: By the end you can understand classroom instructions and short messages (notes, texts) and ask for help when you don't understand.
en-a1-u11-l05.warmup: In a class, on a note stuck on the fridge or in a text message, English is short and direct. Let's read it and use it.
en-a1-u11-l05.topic: Classroom instructions, survival phrases and short messages
md: **Instructions: the imperative (base verb, no subject)**
*Sit down. · Open your book. · Listen and repeat. · Read the text. · Write your name. · Look at the board.*
**Negative:** *Don't use your phone.* · **Polite:** *Please sit down.*
**Survival phrases for class**
| I want… | I say… |
| them to repeat it | *Can you repeat that, please?* |
| them to speak more slowly | *Can you speak more slowly, please?* |
| to say I don't understand | *I don't understand.* |
| to know what it means | *What does 'wallet' mean?* |
| to know how to say it | *How do you say … in English?* |
| to know how it's spelt | *How do you spell it?* |
**Short messages**
- **Notes:** *Back at six. · Gone to the shop. · Please close the window.* (words are left out: *I'll be back at six*)
- **Text messages:** *Where are you? · I'm at the café. · See you soon! · Running late.*
Careful: the imperative has no *to*: *Open the door* (not *To open the door*). *Don't* + base verb: *Don't talk.*
Pronunciation: *listen* /ˈlɪsn/ (the t is silent) · *repeat* /rɪˈpiːt/.
mist: The imperative has no to.
Negative with don't.

en-a1-u11-l06.title: A1 final checkpoint
en-a1-u11-l06.objective: By the end you show A1 level: you name objects, use articles, locate things, understand instructions and sort vocabulary.
en-a1-u11-l06.warmup: A1 final checkpoint: bring together objects, articles, places, instructions and the topics of the whole level.
en-a1-u11-l06.recap: Review: everyday objects, What's this?, a / an / the, Where's…?, instructions and short messages.
md: **Unit 11 review**
- *pen · notebook · keys · wallet · glasses (plural)*
- *What's this? — It's a … · What are these? — They're …*
- *a dog · the dog · I like music (no article)*
- *Where's my phone? · Where are my keys? · in · on · under · behind*
- *Open your book. · Don't use your phone. · Can you repeat that, please?*
